chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan from Abu Sa'id from Abu Jamil al-Basri who said:

I was with Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman in Baghdad, and I was walking with him in the market. The owner of the vinegar jar opened his jar, and vinegar splashed onto Yunus. I saw him become upset because of it until the sun set. I said to him, 'Why do you not pray?' He said, 'I do not wish to pray until I return home and wash this vinegar from my garment.' I said to him, 'Is this your own opinion or something you have narrated?' He said, 'Hisham ibn al-Hakam informed me that he asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about vinegar, and he said, 'Do not drink it, for it is unknown wine (khamar majhul). And if it touches your garment, wash it.'

key_terms.أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)
key_terms.خَمْرٌ مَجْهُولٌ: Unknown wine (a technical term for vinegar, considered impure)
key_terms.يُونُسَ بْنِ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ: Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, a prominent companion

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on vinegar in Shia jurisprudence regarding ritual purity and prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Istibsar* illustrates the practical application of ritual purity (*taharah*) through the narrative of Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman delaying prayer due to vinegar splashing on his garment. It highlights the scholarly distinction made by Imam al-Sadiq (AS), who classified vinegar as 'unknown wine' (*khamar majhul*) and ritually impure (*najis*), thereby necessitating the washing of clothes before prayer. This incident underscores the Shia emphasis on meticulous attention to minor impurities and the authority of the Imams in defining the status of common consumables.
